clips.text_zh: 我終於醒悟。Crypto死咗。一直做100% ETH baggie，同我啲「毒」結婚咗，落命喺「ETH去10K」呢啲傻逼敘事。依家冇tokenization，冇新錢流入乜都冇。Ethereum根本冇用，永遠唔會被採用。又係學費，但至少唔再問「ETH幾時返10K」。
clips.text_en_b1: I finally realized: crypto is dead. I've been a 100% ETH baggie for so long, completely married to my bags, believing in stupid made-up narratives that would send ETH to $10K. In the past couple of weeks, I realized it is never going to happen. No tokenization, no more money coming in, nothing. Ethereum does nothing.
clips.text_en_b2: I've finally come to my senses: crypto is dead. For years I was a 100% ETH bagholder, emotionally married to my bags and convinced by endless narratives that ETH would inevitably reach $10K. Over the past couple of weeks, I've accepted that this is never going to happen. There is no meaningful tokenization story, no fresh capital flowing in, and nothing left to justify the valuation. Ethereum does basically nothing, and it will never be adopted for anything serious.
clips.text_en_c1: I've finally come around to it: crypto is dead. For years I was a 100 percent ETH bagholder, thoroughly married to my position, and I believed every fabricated narrative that promised ETH would print $10K. Over the past couple of weeks, though, it has become painfully obvious that it is never going to happen. No tokenization story, no fresh inflows of capital, no catalyst whatsoever. Ethereum does nothing useful; it is a science project built by a roomful of assholes sniffing their own farts, and it will never be adopted for anything meaningful. Fine, tuition paid.
clips.text_en_c2: I have finally reached the point of clarity: crypto is dead. For years, I was a 100 percent ETH bagholder, emotionally married to my position and convinced that elaborate narratives about tokenization, adoption, and institutional money would eventually propel ETH to $10,000. In the past couple of weeks, however, the flow of new capital has dried up, and the promised use cases have failed to materialize. Ethereum, in practical terms, does almost nothing; it remains a sprawling science project built by people who appear to have mistaken their own fart jokes for a technological vision. Nothing will be adopted at scale. Perhaps I have merely paid an expensive tuition fee, but at least I no longer ask when ETH will return to $10,000.
clips.source_hint: A /biz/ post about abandoning Ethereum and its $10K dream.

clips.text_zh: 我做day trading第三日，而家整緊backtesting、forward testing同paper trading bot。我係咪傻，定其實做法啱？靠AI續命，個bot未ready已經先當transformation signal。
clips.text_en_b1: It's my third day learning day trading, and I'm making a backtesting, forward-testing, and paper-trading bot. Am I being retarded, or am I doing it right? This is what I saw on /biz/ today.
clips.text_en_b2: I'm on the third day of learning day trading, and somehow I've already started building a bot that handles backtesting, forward testing, and paper trading. Am I completely out of my mind, or is this actually the right way to approach it? These days you can lean on AI to keep the project alive, even before the bot is genuinely ready. It already treats something like a transformation signal, which feels slightly absurd.
clips.text_en_c1: Today marks my third day learning day trading, and I am currently assembling a bot that handles backtesting, forward testing, and paper trading. The question nagging at me is whether I am simply being retarded or whether, by some unlikely chance, I am doing this correctly. I am keeping the thing alive with AI assistance, because the bot is not even ready yet and I have already started treating every transformation signal as gospel. This is what /biz/ was discussing today, and I would genuinely appreciate someone telling me whether this is how it is supposed to work.
clips.text_en_c2: It is only my third day learning day trading, and I am already building a bot that conducts backtesting, forward testing, and paper trading. I am using AI to sustain the effort before the system is even remotely ready, while treating it as a transformation signal rather than a finished trading strategy. Am I being naive, or is this broadly the correct way to proceed? The process feels wildly accelerated, particularly because a functioning bot requires careful historical validation, realistic assumptions about execution, and safeguards against overfitting. Nevertheless, I am taking the first tentative steps, which is more than most beginners manage. This is what appeared on /biz/ today.
clips.source_hint: A beginner describes building a day-trading test bot.

clips.text_zh: Nvidia新CEO上任。Rajit Bhamra接任，做AI晶片王嘅工程主管。廢柴如我都要睇多兩眼：工程背景頂到最前，係咪代表NVIDIA由engineering-first行落去？AI接job嘅壓力又加多一層。
clips.text_en_b1: New CEO appointed. Nvidia Corp. appointed Rajit Bhamra as Chief Executive Officer, placing the veteran engineering leader in charge of the biggest company on Earth. Operating from the chipmaker's Santa Clara headquarters, he assumes command of the multi-trillion-dollar artificial intelligence giant whose processors and software platforms power the modern computing economy. He was born in a village in India.
clips.text_en_b2: Nvidia has appointed a new CEO: Rajit Bhamra, the veteran engineering executive who has spent years overseeing the company's AI chips. Even someone as hopeless as me has to take notice, because promoting the head of engineering to the top suggests NVIDIA may finally be shifting away from its engineering-first identity. At the same time, the pressure of competing for jobs against AI keeps growing. The company is enormous, but its strategy now seems tied tightly to one very narrow market.
clips.text_en_c1: New CEO appointed. Nvidia Corp. has named Rajit Bhamra Chief Executive Officer, putting the veteran engineering leader in charge of the biggest company on Earth. Operating out of the chipmaker's Santa Clara headquarters, he now assumes command of a multi-trillion-dollar artificial intelligence giant whose processors and software platforms power the modern computing economy. Even a useless dilettante like me has to take a second look at this: an engineering pedigree pushed to the very top of the organization, which raises the question of whether Nvidia is quietly moving away from its engineering-first identity. Whatever the case, the pressure on AI's new custodian has just increased by another layer.
clips.text_en_c2: Nvidia has appointed Rajit Bhamra as its new Chief Executive Officer, entrusting the veteran engineering leader with the responsibility of running what is now the world’s largest company by market value. Operating from Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters, he will oversee a multitrillion-dollar artificial-intelligence enterprise whose processors and software platforms underpin much of the modern computing economy. The appointment is significant because an engineer with decades of technical experience is taking charge at a moment when AI infrastructure has become strategically indispensable. Even someone as incurably mediocre as I am must take notice. Does his elevation signal that Nvidia remains engineering-first, or that the company is becoming a more conventional, commercially driven corporation? The pressure attached to the role is unquestionably immense.
clips.source_hint: A Bloomberg-based /biz/ post about Nvidia appointing Rajit Bhamra as CEO.

clips.text_zh: Jensen如果而家辭職，個名只剩「處理relationship問題走人嘅廢物」。留低，最多係一行footnote。佢就係NVIDIA，冇人替代到。走咗去玩golf？我諗AI empire仲需要工程腦，唔係只靠新聞稿。
clips.text_en_b1: He resigned. The retard should never have fallen for the pressure. Musk has 10 scandals a week and walks off scot-free every time. Nobody remembers them because his work overshadows them. If Jensen walks away now, he'll forever be known as the adulterer fuckup that walked away. If he stays, it'll be a footnote. He is the company. He made it.
clips.text_en_b2: He resigned, because the retard shouldn't have fallen for all that pressure in the first place. Musk gets away with ten scandals a week simply because his work overshadows every one of them. If Jensen walks away now, he'll be remembered forever as the adulterer fuckup who quit. If he stays, his tenure becomes a footnote at best. He is NVIDIA; nobody can replace him, because he built the company into what it is.
clips.text_en_c1: He resigned. The retard should never have succumbed to the pressure in the first place. Musk generates ten scandals a week and walks away scot-free every single time, because nobody remembers them; his work overshadows them all. If Jensen walks now, he will forever be remembered as the adulterer fuckup who walked away. If he stays, then he is a footnote at best. He is the company, and he made it. What the fuck is he going to do now, retire to a golf course? I remain convinced that the AI empire still needs an engineering brain in the room, not someone who lives off press releases.
clips.text_en_c2: Jensen Huang has resigned. He should never have yielded to the pressure in the first place. Musk produces ten scandals every week and strolls away without consequence, because his output eclipses the reputational wreckage. If Jensen walks away now, his legacy will crystallize as that of the adulterous executive who abandoned the company; if he stays, the whole episode may become no more than a footnote. He is Nvidia. He built the institution that bears his name, and nobody can genuinely replace him. His successors can issue polished statements, but they cannot replicate the engineering judgment, industry relationships, and institutional authority accumulated over decades. So what exactly is he going to do now? Play golf while the AI empire still requires a genuine engineering brain rather than press releases?
clips.source_hint: A /g/ thread debating Jensen Huang leaving Nvidia.

clips.text_zh: Sony發明Blu-ray，collect licensing royalties 20年，專利到期收乾就announce exit。大家以為佢哋暗地研究200GB+ successor，結果入到R&D都冇乜。科技最怕唔做，唔係最怕失敗。靠AI續命靠晒。
clips.text_en_b1: Sony invents Blu-ray, collects licensing royalties for 20 years, then the patents expire and the royalties dry up. Sony announces its exit from Blu-ray production. Everyone assumes Sony was researching a successor, like a 200GB-plus optical disc. Then you look inside Sony's R&D: nothing now. When your $300 hard drive fails, you have another option. This came up on /g/ today.
clips.text_en_b2: Sony invented Blu-ray, collected licensing royalties for twenty years, and then, once the patents expired and the money dried up, announced its exit from production. Naturally, everyone assumed Sony had been quietly developing a successor, perhaps a 200GB-plus optical disc. But when you actually look inside Sony's R&D, there is essentially nothing. The terrifying part about technology isn't failure; it's simply doing nothing. Meanwhile, when your $300 hard drive dies, you have another option. This came up on /g/ today.
clips.text_en_c1: Sony invents Blu-ray, collects licensing royalties for twenty years, and then the patents expire and the royalties dry up, so Sony announces its exit from optical disc production. Everyone assumes that behind the curtain, Sony has been quietly researching a successor: some 200GB-plus optical format of our own. Then you peer inside Sony's R&D and find nothing whatsoever. Which is the real lesson here: technology dies from inaction far more often than from failure. When your $300 hard drive eventually fails, you will have no alternative at all. This came up on /g/ today, and the timing is not exactly flattering.
clips.text_en_c2: Sony invented Blu-ray, collected licensing royalties from it for two decades, and then announced its exit from optical-disc production as the relevant patents expired and the revenue stream dried up. Naturally, everyone assumed the company was secretly developing a successor capable of holding more than 200GB. Yet a glance inside Sony’s R&D effort reveals little more than inertia and empty promise. When a $300 hard drive finally fails, consumers will have no optical alternative worth mentioning. The deeper problem is not that Sony’s attempt failed, but that it stopped trying. Technological leadership is sustained by continued investment, not by commemorative slides about past achievements. This observation surfaced on /g/ today, and it is difficult to see where the next practical successor will come from.
clips.source_hint: A /g/ post about Sony leaving optical discs behind.

clips.text_zh: 點解大部分billionaires咁粗俗又冇想像力？以前有Howard Hughes，估係真係推動人類進步嗰種人。而家得Elon好似仲有試。幾百B USD拎出嚟，搞endowment、搞20年太空研究站、甚至免學費college都得。Money先，啲plan先係proof。
clips.text_en_b1: Why are most billionaires so crass and unimaginative? Where are the Howard Hughes and other industrialists pushing mankind forward? Elon is the only one who seems to try. For the hundreds of billions they throw around, they could create an endowment and a 20-year plan to build a mega research station in space, or build new colleges that research their interests with a fully tuition-free…
clips.text_en_b2: Why are so many billionaires crass, unimaginative, and obsessed with accumulating more money rather than pushing humanity forward? Where are the modern Howard Hugheses? Elon seems to be the only one still trying, because for the hundreds of billions they throw around, they could easily fund an endowment and a 20-year plan for a massive research station in space, or build entirely tuition-free colleges dedicated to their own interests. But they don't, which makes you wonder what happened to their ambition along the way.
clips.text_en_c1: Why are most billionaires so crass and unimaginative? Where have all the Howard Hughes figures gone, the industrialists who genuinely pushed mankind forward? Elon seems to be the only one still trying. For the hundreds of billions they throw around without much thought, they could establish an endowment and fund a twenty-year plan to build a mega research station in space, or endow new colleges that research their own interests with a fully tuition-free student body. Instead, they do none of it. Money first, and the plans come later, if they come at all. What exactly happened?
clips.text_en_c2: Why are so many billionaires vulgar, self-indulgent, and astonishingly unimaginative? Where are the modern equivalents of Howard Hughes and other industrialists who genuinely pushed civilization forward? Elon, at least, appears willing to try. Given the hundreds of billions of dollars they deploy so freely, billionaires could establish substantial endowments, commission a twenty-year programme to construct a major research station in space, or create new colleges devoted to their interests and offer them tuition-free. They rarely do. Instead, conspicuous consumption, private jets, and impulsive acquisition dominate the public imagination. Money, however, is not a plan; it merely supplies the raw material. The proof of ambition lies in converting resources into durable institutions capable of producing knowledge long after the donor’s personal reputation has faded.
clips.source_hint: A /pol/ thread asking why billionaires do not fund long-term science projects.

clips.text_zh: Splits廢用，除非時間逼到冇得揀。全身練3至5次一星期完全冇問題：OHP、bench、DL、squat、pullup加accessories放同一節。肥仔信今日又叫我去gym，靠AI續命靠晒，至少重訓嘅重量係真實。
clips.text_en_b1: Splits are retarded unless they are necessary due to time constraints. There is literally nothing wrong with doing full-body training 3 to 5 times a week. There is nothing wrong with doing OHP, bench, deadlift, squat, pull-ups, and various accessories in the same session. My full session looks like this: pull-ups to failure, OHP 5x5, more pull-ups, deadlift 5x1, bench 5x5, squat 3x5.
clips.text_en_b2: Splits are pointless unless time constraints genuinely force them onto you, because there is absolutely nothing wrong with training the whole body three to five times a week. You can perform OHP, bench press, deadlifts, squats, pull-ups, and various accessories within the same session without any real problem. My own full-body session looks like this: pull-ups to failure, OHP 5x5, more pull-ups, deadlift 5x1, bench 5x5, and squat 3x5. As long as the weights keep going up, the results speak for themselves.
clips.text_en_c1: Splits are retarded unless time constraints leave you with no other option. There is literally nothing wrong with training full-body three to five times a week, and nothing wrong whatsoever with pressing OHP, bench, deadlift, squat, pull-ups, and assorted accessories inside the same session. My own full session runs roughly like this: pull-ups to failure, OHP 5x5, more pull-ups, deadlift 5x1, bench 5x5, and squat 3x5. A fat guy at the gym told me today that I should be doing splits, which is a rich recommendation from a man who keeps his progress alive with AI assistance. At least the weights I am putting up are real.
clips.text_en_c2: Body splits are largely unnecessary unless severe time constraints leave you with no alternative. There is nothing inherently wrong with training the entire body three to five times per week, nor with combining the overhead press, bench press, deadlift, squat, pull-ups, and supporting accessories in a single session. My own routine runs as follows: pull-ups to failure, overhead press five sets of five, additional pull-ups, deadlift five sets of one, bench press five sets of five, and squat three sets of five. The sequencing may look unconventional, but the principle is entirely sound: each session develops the body comprehensively rather than fragmenting it into narrow weekly priorities. Progress comes from consistent volume, appropriate loading, recovery, and gradual progression. The weights I record after each hard set are, at least, something real.
clips.source_hint: A /fit/ thread defending frequent full-body workouts over split routines.

clips.text_zh: Eren嘅genocide plan成功，Zeke嘅euthanasia plan都成功。兩套計畫都「work」，但humanity死晒八成，Eldians又冇晒power of titan，全世界更加恨佢哋。係Isayama被逼寫咁差？定係AoT由頭到尾就爛，係我哋當年冇睇出？
clips.text_en_b1: Zeke's euthanasia plan works. Eren's genocide plan works. Both plans are great, yet we somehow end with 80% of humans wiped out. Eldians are now left without power of Titan shifting, and the whole world hates them 100 times more. Was Isayama threatened into making such a shitty ending, or was AoT bad from the start and we just didn't notice?
clips.text_en_b2: Zeke's euthanasia plan succeeds, and Eren's genocide plan succeeds as well, so somehow both ideas work out despite being completely opposed. The result, however, is that 80% of humanity is wiped out, the Eldians lose their power of Titan shifting entirely, and the rest of the world ends up hating them a hundred times more than before. So was Isayama forced into producing such an awful ending, or was Attack on Titan broken from the very beginning, and we were simply too invested to notice?
clips.text_en_c1: Zeke's euthanasia plan works, and Eren's genocide plan works as well. Both schemes are supposedly brilliant, and yet somehow eighty percent of humanity is wiped out in the process. The Eldians are left without the power of Titan shifting, and the rest of the world now hates them a hundred times more than before. Which raises the obvious question: was Isayama pressured into writing such an atrocious ending, or was Attack on Titan rotten from the very first chapter and none of us noticed at the time?
clips.text_en_c2: Zeke’s euthanasia plan succeeds, and Eren’s genocide plan succeeds; somehow, both schemes are presented as workable even though humanity is reduced by eighty percent and the Eldians lose the power of the Titans. The world emerges far more hostile toward them than before, which makes the conclusion difficult to reconcile with the story’s earlier themes. Was Hajime Isayama pressured into writing such an incoherent ending, or was Attack on Titan flawed from its inception, and did audiences simply fail to recognize the rot concealed beneath its dramatic momentum? Both possibilities are dispiriting. If the former, then the ending was an act of creative compromise; if the latter, every promising arc and character development was compromised long before the finale. The ending does not merely disappoint, but actively contradicts much of what preceded it.
clips.source_hint: An /a/ thread debating Attack on Titan's ending and its moral outcomes.
